problem: Imitation-learning VLN agents either generalize poorly (RNN-based) or are too large to deploy (transformer-based), while RL agents trained from sparse environment rewards struggle to learn long-horizon navigation policies from complex instructions.
motivation: RL can overcome dataset limitations and adapt to environment changes, but lacks expert supervision. Decomposing a long instruction into simple sub-instructions lets the agent estimate values faster and learn more efficiently.
key_idea: Use a lightweight open-source LLM to decompose complex navigation instructions into interpretable sub-instructions, then train an RL agent to complete them sequentially, with multi-scale attention (CMA) for textual guidance and a multi-modal fusion discriminator (MFD) to judge sub-instruction completion.
insight: Only the abstract was available, so no ablation evidence can be cited. The abstract's claim is that sub-instruction decomposition gives denser, more interpretable learning signals that speed value estimation under sparse rewards, and that combining scene, object and action cues makes completion judgments more reliable.
method: Instruction decomposition (DILLM-VLN): a lightweight open-source LLM splits a complex instruction into simple interpretable sub-instructions.
Sequential RL training: the RL agent is trained to complete the sub-instructions one after another.
Cascaded multi-scale attention (CMA): integrates instruction features at different scales to give precise textual guidance.
Multi-modal fusion discriminator (MFD): fuses scene, object and action information to assess whether a sub-instruction has been completed.

setting.backbone: lightweight open-source LLM (for decomposition) + RL agent with CMA and MFD (details not given in the abstract)

results: The abstract only states that DILLM-VLN significantly improves baseline performance, with no numbers and no named baselines.
limitations: Only the abstract was available, so benchmark, metrics and setup details are unknown.
The method depends on the quality of the LLM's instruction decomposition (an inference, not stated).
